extracted.intended_audience: copyright claimants, respondents, attorneys, and other participants (including pro se parties) in Copyright Claims Board (CCB) proceedings
extracted.subtask_short: CCB procedural rules and discovery limits
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing management of proceedings, filing limits, written submissions, discovery, evidence, consolidation/severance, settlement, records/publication, and related procedural aspects of CCB cases under the CASE Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on number of proceedings per claimant
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office is authorized to limit the permitted number of proceedings each year by the same claimant. The final rule raises the limit to 30 proceedings in a 12-month period (from the NPRM's proposed 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting filed claims (rather than active cases) is administratively manageable because compliance review occurs at filing and it can be impossible at filing to determine when or whether a case will become active. Raising the limit increases opportunities for cases to be resolved on the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on number of proceedings per attorney and law firm
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule imposes limits on counsel: 40 proceedings per attorney in a 12-month period, and 80 proceedings per law firm in a 12-month period (adjusted from proposed values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limits are intended to prevent abusive monopolization of CCB resources. If an attorney or law firm files a claim that exceeds its limit, that attorney or law firm must withdraw. The CCB may issue a 60-day stay to allow substitution of counsel or proceeding pro se, which may be extended for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for exceeding claimant or counsel limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that exceeds a claimant's limit will be dismissed without prejudice. If an attorney or law firm exceeds its limit by filing a new claim, they must withdraw and the CCB may stay proceedings for 60 days to allow substitution or pro se representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedures mitigate prejudice to claimants while enforcing filing limits; the stay may be extended for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and purpose of filing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The CASE Act and its legislative history authorize limitations to prevent abusive conduct and provide for efficient administration of the CCB (including dismissal when the number or complexity of claims exceeds what the Board could reasonably administer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits are justified to maximize the number of claimants served and prevent a few parties or firms from monopolizing the forum; the Office will review limits in practice and revisit as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB is not bound by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure or the Federal Rules of Evidence; references were removed except to state that the CCB is not bound by those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures are intended to be more flexible, accessible, and permissive than Federal court rules, particularly to accommodate non-lawyers and pro se participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered system for written requests and filings (formatting and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Written requests are streamlined into three tiers: tier one uses a fillable form with a 4,000 character limit and a 7-day response time; tier two uses a fillable form with a 10,000 character limit and a 14-day response time; tier three is for more substantial submissions (e.g., party statements) uploaded to eCCB with standardized formatting, page limits, and response times where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach avoids page/font/formatting burdens for most requests and creates predictable, consistent response times. Tier three submissions will have more formalized formatting and page limits in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling order modification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When an oral request to modify a scheduling order is made at a hearing or conference, other parties may respond orally at that time or request a reasonable amount of time to submit a written response. Written submissions related to scheduling order modifications fall into the fillable form tier system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tier system clarifies timing and response expectations and addresses prior silence in the proposed rule about oral-request response timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amending claims and counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Amended claims or counterclaims are subject to compliance review; amending a claim after service is prohibited without leave of the CCB. Amendments are prohibited during the opt-out period. A claim found noncompliant during compliance review may be freely amended; if leave to amend is granted, the pleading may only be amended as identified in the request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibiting amendments during the opt-out period avoids additional compliance review, service burdens, delay, and administrative difficulty. Written requests for leave to amend fall into the fillable form tier system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and severance rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not include a general severance provision (statute already prevents multiple disparate claims in one proceeding). Consolidation is permitted to combine certain procedural steps (discovery, evidence submission, hearings) for multiple proceedings filed by a claimant against the same respondent when they arise out of the same facts or circumstances, but separate determinations and damages caps remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation is a docket-management tool reserved to the CCB; it is limited to procedural efficiencies and will not join claims into a single proceeding that would circumvent statutory damages caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement procedures and settlement officer recusal
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB shall 'facilitate' (not 'encourage') settlement. The Officer presiding over a settlement conference must recuse from the final determination unless required to act as a tiebreaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change to 'facilitate' aligns with statutory text and addresses concerns about mandating settlement or converting the CCB into a settlement-collection process. Parties should 'send' position statements (not formally 'serve') before settlement conferences to avoid formal service requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public records and transcripts policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Final determinations will be available on a publicly-accessible website; the Office does not currently intend to publish uncorrected raw hearing transcripts as part of the official record (parties may request and pay for an official reporter). The eCCB will allow searches of information about parties and attorneys, including orders related to bad faith. Attendance at hearings is limited to parties and their representatives except with leave of the CCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office seeks to balance transparency with confidentiality and practical/technological/security concerns posed by virtual proceedings; the Office may reevaluate transcript and public-access policies over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized discovery and scope limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will use limited, standardized discovery (interrogatories and document requests) tailored to be narrower than Federal rules. Parties may seek additional discovery on a case-by-case showing of good cause. Standardized discovery reduces burden for pro se parties while capturing common issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties concerned about overbreadth may raise issues at the pre-discovery conference; the CCB Handbook and Copyright Claims Attorneys will provide guidance and examples to make the process understandable to pro se participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to preserve and update discovery responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation imposes a duty to preserve all material documents and to update information provided in response to interrogatories and document requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These duties will be addressed in the CCB Handbook and in pre- and post-discovery conferences; parties should expect preservation obligations and potential reminders for filing-triggered deadlines via eCCB where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer requirement for discovery disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are required to meet and confer regarding discovery disputes before raising the issue with the CCB, though failure to confer will not prevent the CCB from addressing disputes when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reasonable efforts to confer are frustrated, a party may explain the steps taken to resolve the dispute when requesting a conference; the Office is attentive to ensuring the meet-and-confer is not used to avoid addressing disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of discovery responses and documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing parties must certify that interrogatory responses are accurate and truthful and that documents produced are genuine and unaltered to the best of that party's knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will provide specific certification language in the CCB Handbook and on CCB forms. The Office declined to lengthen the certification to include review of protective orders to keep the certification easy to use for all parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule incorporates amendments to protective order procedures: categories of discovery material subject to 'confidential' designation may include undisclosed advertising plans; parties 'must' attempt to resolve disputes over confidentiality designations before bringing such disputes to the CCB; the affected party will have a chance to object before unilateral de-designation by the CCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CCB will be tasked with ensuring protective order procedures are not misused against pro se parties and that confidentiality disputes are meaningfully addressed between parties first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard interrogatories (form and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCB will employ standard form interrogatories using easy-to-understand language; the rule describes interrogatory categories but not their final text, which will be finalized for clarity and usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office reviewed and simplified language to assist both attorneys and pro se parties. Media-specific versions of standardized interrogatories are not required at this time but may be considered in the future; parties needing media-specific discovery may request it under the additional discovery process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'material' documents
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'material' document is one that could be used to prove or disprove a fact that is in dispute in a proceeding and may have influence on the outcome of the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'material' documents are potentially unlimited, the Office will provide guidance and examples in the CCB Handbook rather than a regulatory list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for admission are limited and discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for admission (RFAs) are classified as a form of additional discovery and will be allowed only 'on a limited basis' and 'for good cause shown'—they will not be available as of right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule responds to concerns about RFAs' complexity and burden for pro se parties; requesting parties must provide the specific RFAs they seek and show good cause for each. The NPRM's proposed ten-request limit and ban on compound requests informed this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of financial and other documents 'sufficient to show'
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid overbroad burdens, financial document requests (e.g., revenues, profits, deductible expenses) have been revised so responding parties are required to produce only 'documents sufficient to show' those matters rather than all documents 'related to' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation safeguards against overbroad discovery while allowing relevant evidence (including licensing history) to be discovered when appropriate. For misrepresentation claims, the Office rejected a proposal that would permit producing only exculpatory documents and requires production of documents 'pertaining to' assertions where necessary to assess truth or falsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery for specialized claims (e.g., section 512(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties asserting or defending specialized claims (such as section 512(f) misrepresentation claims) may seek additional interrogatories or discovery, but must do so under the process for additional discovery and show good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office declined to waive the good-cause requirement for initial additional discovery in section 512(f) claims, reasoning that additional information needs can be addressed through the existing additional discovery process rather than an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad-faith findings and penalties; publication policy for bad-faith actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The CASE Act prescribes penalties for bad-faith determinations; CCB may award attorney's fees. The Office considered but did not adopt a public list of bad-faith actors, viewing it as unduly harsh; however, CCB determinations and orders (including any orders related to bad faith) will be public and searchable via eCCB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office believes available penalties (including fee awards) and public availability of determinations provide consequences for bad faith without creating a separate public 'bad-faith list' at this time.
